questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the Common Service Data Model (CSDM)?

options.text: To replace the CMDB with a new database structure
To provide guidance on where to place data in ServiceNow for maximum value
To install new applications that manage service data
To create custom tables for each customer's unique needs

explanation.correct: CSDM is guidance on where to put data inside of ServiceNow to get the most value out of your investment. It is not a SKU or product to purchase, but free guidance on data placement and structure. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-overview.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: CSDM does not replace the CMDB. It provides guidance on how to use the CMDB and other tables effectively.
CSDM is not a product or application to install. It's guidance documentation that can be implemented using existing platform capabilities.
CSDM provides standardized guidance using out-of-box tables, not custom tables. Customization often leads to technical debt.

source.excerpt: CSDM is guidance on, where do I need to put data inside of ServiceNow to get the most value out of my investment of ServiceNow? It's not a SKU or a product that we sell. This is absolutely free guidance.

questions.question: What is 'technical debt' in the context of CSDM implementation?

options.text: The cost of purchasing ServiceNow licenses
The effort required to rework customizations that don't align with CSDM standards
The time needed to train users on new features
The budget allocated for IT infrastructure upgrades

explanation.correct: Technical debt in CSDM context refers to the cost and effort required to rework customizations that don't follow CSDM guidance. When organizations create customizations instead of using out-of-box capabilities, they accumulate technical debt that prevents them from leveraging new platform capabilities. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-technical-debt.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: License costs are separate from technical debt. Technical debt is about rework effort from non-standard implementations.
Training time is not technical debt. Technical debt specifically refers to the effort to correct implementations that deviate from standards.
Infrastructure budget is not technical debt. Technical debt is the accumulated cost of taking shortcuts in implementation.

source.excerpt: When you look at that effort that it takes to rework something that you've implemented and all the dependencies that you've created on what you've implemented, you really want to be careful of those customizations, because that cost of effort can be quite vast.

questions.question: Which three pillars are essential for managing data successfully according to CSDM? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Ingest - bringing data into the system
Govern - managing data lifecycle and structure
Insight - using data for operational and strategic activities
Export - sending data to external systems

explanation.correct: The three key pillars for managing data successfully in CSDM are: Ingest (bringing data in from automation or manual sources), Govern (managing the lifecycle and structure of data with CSDM at the center), and Insight (using the data for operational, planning, and strategic activities). See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-data-management.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Export is not one of the three core pillars. The pillars are Ingest, Govern, and Insight. While data may be exported, the focus is on bringing data in and using it effectively.

source.excerpt: You need to ingest information into the system from either automation sources or manual sources that are governed to a large degree. And you need to govern the life cycle of that data and the structure of that data... Insight really gets down into, how do you need to leverage this information.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the Application table (cmdb_ci_appl) and the Business Application table in ServiceNow?

options.text: They are the same table with different labels
Application is for discovered software installations; Business Application is for the portfolio of applications
Business Application is for internal apps; Application is for external apps
Application requires a license; Business Application is free to use

explanation.correct: The Application table (cmdb_ci_appl) is populated by Discovery with installed software (bits and bytes) found on hosts. The Business Application table represents your organization's portfolio of applications for planning and enterprise architecture purposes, and is version-agnostic. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-application-tables.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: These are distinct tables with different purposes. The Application table is cmdb_ci_appl for discovered software, while Business Application is a separate table for portfolio management.

The distinction is not about internal vs external. Application is for discovered installed software, Business Application is for your application portfolio regardless of whether it's internal or external.
Both tables are available without additional licensing. The distinction is about purpose and how data is populated.

source.excerpt: The purpose of the application table was really devoted to discovery. Discovery would populate that table... based off of what it sees from an installation standpoint... The business application... was a new table that was needed in order to identify our portfolio of applications.

questions.question: What is an Application Service in CSDM and why is it considered one of the most important objects?

options.text: A cloud-hosted application that ServiceNow manages
A deployed instance of a business application used for operational impact analysis
A service ticket category for application-related issues
A backup copy of a business application for disaster recovery

explanation.correct: Application Service represents a deployed instance of a business application (e.g., dev, QA, prod environments). It's critical because it's the operational CI used in incident, problem, and change management for impact analysis - showing what business services are affected when technology has issues. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-application-service.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Application Service is not about cloud hosting. It represents deployed instances of business applications in any environment.
Application Service is a CI type in the CMDB, not a ticket category. It's used to identify deployed application instances.
Application Service represents production instances, not backups. Each environment (dev, QA, prod) would be a separate Application Service.

source.excerpt: The application service is probably one of the most important objects in the common service data model. It's a service instance type. And this is meant to identify the instance of a business application... this is what we want to know has impact when it comes from a service management perspective.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Ideation and Strategy domain introduced in CSDM 5?

options.text: To manage incident tickets related to strategy meetings
To capture product ideas and strategic planning before development begins
To store user feedback after services are deployed
To track service level agreements for strategic services

explanation.correct: The Ideation and Strategy domain is new in CSDM 5 and captures where ideas begin. It includes product ideas, strategic planning objects like mission, vision, and value identification, and goals - enabling better business decisions about what to green-light or hold off. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-ideation-strategy.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Incident management is handled in the Service Delivery domain. Ideation and Strategy is about capturing ideas before they become projects.
User feedback collection would be in Service Consumption. Ideation and Strategy is the beginning of the lifecycle, before deployment.
SLAs are managed in Service Consumption. Ideation and Strategy focuses on initial ideas and strategic planning.

source.excerpt: This is where ideas begin... product ideas and being able to plan those product ideas... Once we have these ideas, what do we do strategically to plan for these moving forward and understand, what's its mission? What's its vision? What's its value to the organization?

questions.question: What does the Business Capability object in the Design and Planning domain represent?

options.text: The technical specifications of a software application
What your company does, decomposed into subcapabilities for planning
The list of users who can access business applications
The hardware capacity requirements for running services

explanation.correct: Business Capability represents what your company does and is used in capability-based planning. It can be decomposed into subcapabilities and helps identify people, processes, and technology needed to do work. This is used for strategic planning decisions about technology or skill investments. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-design-planning.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Technical specifications belong in the Build and Integrate or Service Delivery domains. Business Capability is a strategic planning concept.
User access is managed through roles and groups, not Business Capability. Business Capability represents organizational functions.
Hardware capacity is tracked in the CMDB under infrastructure CIs. Business Capability is about organizational functions, not technical capacity.

source.excerpt: We have something called the business capability. The best way to describe this, this is what your company does. And it is usually used in capability-based planning. You decompose those down into subcapabilities.

questions.question: Which attribute has replaced the 'use_for' field for identifying CI environments (dev, QA, prod) in CSDM?

options.text: lifecycle_stage
environment
install_status
stage_status

explanation.correct: The 'use_for' attribute was historically used to identify environments (dev, QA, prod) but was not available on all CIs. It has been replaced by the 'environment' attribute, which provides consistent environment identification across all CI types. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-deprecated.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: lifecycle_stage is for tracking the CI's stage in its lifecycle (build, operational, end of life), not its deployment environment.
install_status is a legacy status field being deprecated in favor of lifecycle stage/status. It does not replace use_for.
stage_status provides a 'flavor' within a lifecycle stage (e.g., pending retirement within operational), not the deployment environment.

source.excerpt: We have an attribute called use_for, which historically was identifying the environments of a CI, dev QA prod. But use_for was not on all CIs. So we have since replaced that with an attribute called environment.

questions.question: What capability has replaced the use of cmdb_real_group and cmdb_real_group_type tables for identifying groups responsible for CIs?

options.text: Assignment Groups
TEAMs
Support Groups
CI Relationships

explanation.correct: TEAMs is a related list capability on CIs that identifies the unique groups responsible for various elements of a CI - support group, managed group, change group, vulnerability group, development group, etc. It replaces the previous cmdb_real_group and cmdb_real_group_type tables. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-teams.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Assignment Groups are used for assigning work in ITSM processes. TEAMs is the comprehensive solution for identifying all groups responsible for a CI.
Support Groups are just one type of group tracked in TEAMs. TEAMs provides a broader capability including support, change, vulnerability, and development groups.
CI Relationships connect CIs to other CIs. TEAMs connects CIs to groups responsible for different aspects of the CI.

source.excerpt: We've implemented a concept called TEAMs. So this is a related list to a CI to identify the unique groups that are responsible for various elements of that CI... TEAMs has been created as an overall capability-related list to a CI. And it replaces a previous use of cmdb_real_group and cmdb_real_group_type.

questions.question: Why should organizations avoid creating CIs directly in the Base Service class?

options.text: The Base Service class has been completely removed from the platform
Extended dedicated tables (business services, technical services) should be used via Service Builder
The Base Service class requires additional licensing
CIs in the Base Service class cannot have relationships

explanation.correct: The Base Service class has been extended over the years with dedicated tables for business services, technical services, etc. CSDM guidance is to use these extended dedicated tables and Service Builder to create CIs, rather than creating them directly in the Base Service class. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-service-tables.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The Base Service class hasn't been removed - it still exists. However, the extended tables should be used instead of creating CIs directly in the base table.
There is no additional licensing requirement. The recommendation is based on CSDM best practices for proper data organization.
CIs in the Base Service class can have relationships. The issue is that extended tables provide better categorization and alignment with CSDM guidance.

source.excerpt: The Base Service class we have extended. Originally, it was just one service table. And we've extended that over the years. We've got an extension for business services, technical services. And we want to make sure that usage is done at those extended dedicated tables.

questions.question: What has replaced the need for the Software Package and Software Install tables?

options.text: Discovery patterns
SAM Foundations
Application Service records
TEAMs capability

explanation.correct: SAM Foundations has replaced the need for the Software Package and Software Install tables. These tables were part of the original CMDB and the initial APM/SAM iterations. With SAM Foundations installed (which is recommended even without a SAM license), these legacy tables are no longer necessary. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-it-asset-management/page/product/software-asset-management2/concept/c_SoftwareAssetManagement.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Discovery patterns populate CI data but don't replace Software Package/Install functionality. SAM Foundations provides the software management capability.
Application Service represents deployed application instances, not software package management. These are different CSDM concepts.
TEAMs is for group management on CIs, not software package tracking. SAM Foundations handles software asset management.

source.excerpt: With SAM Foundations, it's not necessary to populate and utilize the Software Package table or the Software Install table when you have SAM Foundations inside the platform... we encourage that that is installed for customers.

questions.question: Which implementation approaches for CSDM are recommended? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Outcome-centric - tackling data requirements for a specific outcome
Domain-centric - focusing on a specific area of the model
Stepwise (crawl, walk, run, fly) - legacy approach being moved away from
Big-bang - implementing everything at once

explanation.correct: CSDM recommends outcome-centric (achieving a specific outcome) and domain-centric (tackling a specific area of the model) approaches. The stepwise approach (crawl, walk, run, fly) is being moved away from as it doesn't always provide immediate value, especially for larger organizations. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-implementation.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: While stepwise is still applicable for some scenarios (particularly smaller organizations), ServiceNow is moving away from it as the primary recommendation because it doesn't provide immediate value.
wrongAnswers.reference: CSDM Fundamentals course - Transitioning and Next Steps

wrongAnswers.explanation: Big-bang implementation is not a recommended CSDM approach. CSDM emphasizes iterative approaches focused on outcomes or specific domains.

source.excerpt: The stepwise approach is something we're trying to get away from. While it works in certain scenarios, we find it just doesn't see the results at the level of... investment folks are trying to make.

questions.question: When a new version of CSDM is released (e.g., CSDM 5), what happens to existing CSDM implementations?

options.text: Existing implementations must be completely rebuilt to comply with the new version
CSDM iterates and adds to the model without removing previous work - organizations expand as needed
All tables are renamed and data must be migrated
Previous CSDM versions become unsupported immediately

explanation.correct: CSDM versions iterate rather than replace. Each version adds more to the model, and organizations can look at what pieces are important to their goals and expand from their current implementation. Changes are primarily label changes, and the underlying table functionality remains the same. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/zurich-servicenow-platform/page/product/configuration-management/concept/csdm-versioning.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: You don't have to start over with each CSDM version. ServiceNow works hard to ensure implementations can live in perpetuity with iterative improvements.
wrongAnswers.reference: CSDM Fundamentals course - Transitioning and Next Steps

wrongAnswers.explanation: Tables aren't renamed - they remain the same. Changes are primarily on the label side for management of change. The way tables work hasn't fundamentally changed.
Previous versions remain supported. Organizations on CSDM 3 or 4 can continue their implementations and expand as they see fit.

source.excerpt: What we do with CSDM does not replace what we've already talked about, but we iterate. We add more to it. And so it matures and grows over time. We're not taking anything away... whether you're starting with CSDM 3 or you're starting with CSDM 4, you don't have to stop everything.
